samf-senior-2002-r1-01.title: Read the graph
samf-senior-2002-r1-01.body:
The first runner is the fastest (about 75) and the third runner the slowest (about 90). The difference is about $90-75=15$.

**Answer: (A) 15**

samf-senior-2002-r1-02.title: Pair the terms
samf-senior-2002-r1-02.body:
Group as $(2002-2001)+(2000-1999)+\cdots+(2-1)$: 1001 pairs, each equal to 1. The total is 1001.

**Answer: (D) 1001**

samf-senior-2002-r1-03.title: Average of shifted numbers
samf-senior-2002-r1-03.body:
The new sum is the old sum plus $10\times20=200$; dividing by 10, the average increases by 20.

**Answer: (B)**

samf-senior-2002-r1-04.title: Percentage increase
samf-senior-2002-r1-04.body:
Two small tubes cost R5,98, which is R0,89 more than R5,09. The percentage is $\frac{0{,}89}{5{,}09}\times100\approx\frac{90}{5}=18$.

**Answer: (B) 18**

samf-senior-2002-r1-06.title: Column addition
samf-senior-2002-r1-06.body:
Units: $4+5+7=16$, carry 1. Hundreds: the sum ends in 4, so exactly 2 is carried from the tens column. Tens: $1+P+Q+R=20$, so $P+Q+R=19$. If $R=1$ then $P+Q=18$, forcing $P=Q=9$, not allowed (different digits). Other values work: $R=3$: $P,Q=7,9$; $R=6$: $4,9$; $R=8$: $2,9$; $R=9$: $4,6$.

**Answer: (A) 1**

samf-senior-2002-r1-07.title: Isosceles triangles
samf-senior-2002-r1-07.body:
Each interior angle of the pentagon is $108^\circ$. Triangle $CBD$ is isosceles with apex angle $108^\circ$, so $\angle CDB=\frac12(180^\circ-108^\circ)=36^\circ$; likewise $\angle DCE=36^\circ$. In triangle $DFC$: $\angle DFC=180^\circ-36^\circ-36^\circ=108^\circ$.

**Answer: (B) $108^\circ$**

samf-senior-2002-r1-08.title: Use times
samf-senior-2002-r1-08.body:
Let each half be $D$. Total time at 40 km/h: $\frac{2D}{40}=\frac D{20}$. First half took $\frac D{30}$. Second half must take $\frac D{20}-\frac D{30}=\frac D{60}$, so the speed is 60 km/h.

**Answer: (C) 60 km/h**

samf-senior-2002-r1-08.title: Harmonic mean
samf-senior-2002-r1-08.body:
Average speed over two equal distances is the harmonic mean: $\frac{2}{\frac1{30}+\frac1S}=40$ gives $\frac1S=\frac1{20}-\frac1{30}=\frac1{60}$.

**Answer: (C)**

samf-senior-2002-r1-09.title: Equation
samf-senior-2002-r1-09.body:
With tens digit $T$ and units digit $U$: $10T+U=7(T+U)$, so $3T=6U$, $T=2U$. With $T\le9$ and $T\ge1$: $U=1,2,3,4$ giving $21,42,63,84$. Four numbers.

**Answer: (A) 4**

samf-senior-2002-r1-10.title: Last digits repeat
samf-senior-2002-r1-10.body:
Last digits of powers of 7: 7, 9, 3, 1, then repeat with period 4. $2002=4\cdot500+2$, so the last digit is that of $7^2=49$, i.e. 9.

**Answer: (D) 9**

samf-senior-2002-r1-11.title: Spot the pattern
samf-senior-2002-r1-11.body:
Row $k$ has $k$ numbers, so rows $1,\ldots,k-1$ contain $\frac{k(k-1)}2$ odd numbers. The middle numbers of rows 1, 3, 5 are $1,9,25=1^2,3^2,5^2$. In general the middle of odd row $k$ is $k^2$: row 51 has middle $51^2=2601$.

Check: the first number of row $k$ is the $\left(\frac{k(k-1)}2+1\right)$-th odd number, $k(k-1)+1$; the middle is $\frac{k-1}2$ places later: $k(k-1)+1+(k-1)=k^2$.

**Answer: (A) 2601**

samf-senior-2002-r1-13.title: List
samf-senior-2002-r1-13.body:
$q$ must be odd, and $3q<25$, so $q\in\{1,3,5,7\}$, giving $p=11,8,5,2$. Four pairs.

**Answer: (C) 4**

samf-senior-2002-r1-14.title: Subtract a small triangle
samf-senior-2002-r1-14.body:
Triangle $ACD$ is half the square: $\frac12(7\sqrt2)^2=49$. Triangle $EFC$ has a right angle at $F$ and $\angle FCE=45^\circ$, so it is isosceles with hypotenuse $EC=2\sqrt2$ and legs $EF=FC=2$, area $\frac12\cdot2\cdot2=2$. Then $AFED=49-2=47$.

**Answer: (E) 47**

samf-senior-2002-r1-15.title: Last digits
samf-senior-2002-r1-15.body:
The terms are $1,3,9,33,153,\ldots$. For $n\ge5$, $n!$ ends in 0, so every term from $1!+\cdots+4!=33$ on ends in 3. A perfect square never ends in 3. The only squares are 1 and 9: two.

**Answer: (B) 2**

samf-senior-2002-r1-16.title: Find the centre
samf-senior-2002-r1-16.body:
The triangle has sides 12, 12, 6, so its height is $\sqrt{144-9}=3\sqrt{15}$. The centre lies on the axis of symmetry at distance $r$ from each vertex, hence at distance $3\sqrt{15}-r$ from the midpoint of the base. Then $r^2=3^2+(3\sqrt{15}-r)^2$ gives $6\sqrt{15}\,r=144$, so $r=\frac{24}{\sqrt{15}}=\frac{8\sqrt{15}}5$.

**Answer: (A)**

samf-senior-2002-r1-17.title: Digits must be 1, 1, p
samf-senior-2002-r1-17.body:
A product of three digits is prime only if two digits are 1 and the third is a one-digit prime $p\in\{2,3,5,7\}$. For each $p$ the digits $1,1,p$ can be arranged in 3 ways. Total $4\times3=12$.

**Answer: (B) 12**

samf-senior-2002-r1-18.title: Bound the smallest
samf-senior-2002-r1-18.body:
$\frac1a>\frac1b>\frac1c$, so $\frac1a>\frac13$, hence $a<3$; and $\frac1a<1$ so $a>1$: $a=2$. Then $\frac1b+\frac1c=\frac12$ with $\frac1b>\frac14$ and $\frac1b<\frac12$, so $b=3$ and $c=6$.

**Answer: (A) 6**

samf-senior-2002-r1-19.title: Factorise
samf-senior-2002-r1-19.body:
$n^5-n=n(n^2-1)(n^2+1)=(n-1)n(n+1)(n^2+1)$ is divisible by the product of three consecutive integers $(n-1)n(n+1)$, hence by 2 and by 3, so by 6. Of the options 1, 2, 3, 6, 5 the number 6 is the largest, so it is the answer. (In fact $n^5-n$ is always divisible by 30, but 30 is not offered.)

**Answer: (D) 6**

samf-senior-2002-r1-20.title: Right triangle
samf-senior-2002-r1-20.body:
Let $M$ have radius $r$. Its centre is at distance $1-r$ above the centre of the large semicircle and at distance $\frac12+r$ from the centre of either small semicircle, which is $\frac12$ from the large centre. So $\left(\frac12+r\right)^2=(1-r)^2+\frac14$, giving $r+\frac14=1-2r+\frac14$, i.e. $r=\frac13$.

**Answer: (A) $\frac13$**
